Direct Kinetic Modelling: Application to Combustion Engines

Abstract 
5 
Hydrogen combustion can decarbonise difficult-to-abate sectors. However, practical deployment 
6 
depends on reliable prediction of combustion behaviour under transient conditions, which contrasts 
7 
with the steady-state experiments typically used for combustion mechanism development. This study 
8 
presents a fully optimised H₂-NOₓ mechanism, calibrated against 118 fundamental combustion 
9 
datasets containing 1695 datapoints, which shows significant improvements in the prediction of 
10 
ignition onset in an internal combustion engine with nitric oxide injection into the intake system.  
11 
In contrast to prior single-objective approaches, this study introduces a fundamentally new approach 
12 
to chemical kinetic mechanism optimisation, which leverages a Multi-Objective Particle Swarm 
13 
Optimisation framework on a High-Performance Computing platform. The framework simultaneously 
14 
balances accuracy and consistency across datasets, explicitly incorporates experimental uncertainty, 
15 
and evaluates all candidate mechanisms with full chemical simulations. Prediction accuracy is 
16 
quantified using the normalised root mean square error (nRMSE) to experimental measurements and 
17 
the proportion of predictions within experimental uncertainty limits. Relative to the best existing 
18 
mechanism, the optimised model achieves a 35% reduction in nRMSE and a 19% increase in the 
19 
number of predictions within uncertainty bounds, demonstrating improved predictive performance 
20 
for fundamental combustion targets.  
21 


 
 
2 
 
When the optimised mechanism was applied to autoignition timing in a Homogeneous Charge 
1 
Compression Ignition engine, significant improvements were found for data with nitric oxide. 
2 
Nevertheless, the overall accuracy in autoignition prediction is insufficient for practical applications, 
3 
indicating that transient engine conditions are not adequately represented by steady-state datasets. 
4 
These findings underscore that even fully optimised mechanisms based solely on fundamental 
5 
experiments will not deliver high-accuracy predictions under real-world, transient conditions and 
6 
integration of transient combustion data into future development of chemical mechanisms is 
7 
recommended.

1. Introduction  
12 
The development of clean and efficient energy technologies is central to achieving global 
13 
decarbonisation goals [1], particularly in difficult-to-abate sectors such as transportation, industrial 
14 
heating, and power generation. Hydrogen (H2) is increasingly regarded as a key energy carrier in this 
15 
transition, offering carbon-free combustion and flexibility in integration with renewable energy 
16 
sources [2]. However, the practical implementation of hydrogen-based energy systems, including 
17 
hydrogen internal combustion engines [3, 4], gas turbines [5] and industrial burners [6], requires highly 
18 
accurate and robust models of hydrogen combustion. Such models are essential for system design, 
19 
performance optimisation, emissions control, and safety assurance under a wide range of operating 
20 
conditions. A core component of these models is the hydrogen combustion chemistry, which defines 
21 
the fundamental reaction pathways and governs the ignition behaviours and formation of pollutants 
22 
such as nitrogen oxides (NOx). Thus, the fidelity and prediction accuracy of hydrogen chemical kinetic 
23 
mechanisms are vital for the simulation and optimisation of future energy systems. 
24 


 
 
3 
 
Chemical kinetic mechanisms for hydrogen [7-12] as well as natural gas, syngas, ammonia, and short- 
1 
and long-carbon [13-22] oxidation have been previously developed and used to simulate combustion 
2 
processes across diverse thermochemical conditions. In recent years, automatic mechanism 
3 
generation and reduction techniques [21-25] have been increasingly employed due to their scalability 
4 
and ability to incorporate detailed reaction pathways from expansive chemical spaces while reducing 
5 
human errors. Central to advancing these mechanisms is the accurate characterisation of rate 
6 
parameters, especially under conditions relevant to practical energy systems. Rate parameters are 
7 
typically derived from experimental measurements or theoretical calculations based on quantum 
8 
chemistry, reaction rate or transition state theory [26], all of which carry an uncertainty for the derived 
9 
parameters. These uncertainties can propagate through combustion simulations, affecting the 
10 
reliability of predictions critical to the design and operation of applied energy technologies.  
11 
To improve prediction accuracy, researchers typically follow two approaches, both relying on selecting 
12 
datapoints of interest and conducting sensitivity analysis to identify influential rate parameters. The 
13 
first is a local optimisation approach, where parameter adjustments are guided by expert judgment, 
14 
e.g., [7, 8, 10]. This approach is fast and convenient but relies heavily on author intuition and may yield 
15 
parameter sets that are neither physically consistent nor broadly applicable. As such, the resulting 
16 
mechanisms may fit selected datasets well but lack robustness across broader operating conditions. 
17 
The second approach treats mechanism development as a formal optimisation problem, where 
18 
algorithms and optimisation frameworks are used to systematically adjust kinetic parameters to 
19 
minimise discrepancies between model predictions and experimental data. This approach removes the 
20 
subjectivity associated with expert-guided adjustments by instead exploring the uncertainty 
21 
hyperspace of reaction rate parameters using optimisation algorithms. As a result, it enables the 
22 
development of more generalisable and physically consistent mechanisms across a wide range of 
23 
thermochemical conditions, e.g., [17, 18, 27-31]. However, this method can be computationally 
24 


 
 
4 
 
intensive, particularly when the full chemical kinetic simulations are required for every candidate 
1 
solution during the optimisation process.  
2 
To alleviate the computational requirements of the optimisation, many studies adopt the solution 
3 
mapping approach to generate polynomial surrogate models based on quadratic equations (known as 
4 
“response surfaces”) fit to a sample of mechanism responses – e.g., [12, 17, 30-34]. These response 
5 
surfaces replace the need to conduct the full simulations of experimental data for rapid mechanism 
6 
optimisation but may fail to capture the complex, multi-modal combustion behaviour, introducing 
7 
fitting errors and limiting accuracy [31]. Despite the potential errors, response surfaces have been 
8 
integrated with frameworks such as the Bound-To-Bound Data-Collaboration (B2B-DC) framework [34] 
9 
and the Method of Uncertainty quantification and Minimization using Polynomial Chaos Expansions 
10 
(MUM-PCE) [35] to develop chemical kinetic models [17, 18, 27, 28]. These frameworks handle 
11 
uncertainties from both reaction rate constants and combustion property measurements. Efforts have 
12 
also been made to combine full chemical kinetic simulations with heuristic methods such as 
13 
Evolutionary Algorithms [36, 37], self-adaptive Genetic Algorithms (GAs) [38-41], strengthen elitist GA 
14 
[42], and Particle Swarm Optimisation (PSO) [43, 44]. However, their direct application does not 
15 
address the inherent uncertainties in the kinetic parameters and is computationally expensive, with 
16 
Elliot and co-workers [38-41] reporting a five-day runtime on a single processor core to optimise a 
17 
mechanism against just five laminar flame speed (LFS) datapoints.  These limitations highlight the need 
18 
for a more flexible and robust optimisation framework capable of improving mechanism accuracy and 
19 
fidelity without relying on response surfaces or imposing overly restrictive assumptions. 
20 
To address the inherent limitations of existing optimisation strategies, this paper introduces a 
21 
fundamentally new approach to chemical kinetic mechanism development, which leverages multi-
22 
objective optimisation (MOO) on a High-Performance Computing (HPC) platform. MOO has emerged 
23 
as a powerful tool in combustion systems optimisation for balancing competing objectives across a 
24 
complex parameter space, e.g., in internal combustion engine performance optimisation [45-48], gas 
25 


 
 
5 
 
turbine for power generation optimisation [49-51], and industrial burner optimisation [52-54]. 
1 
Although the chemical kinetic mechanism used controls critical combustion processes in these 
2 
systems, mechanism optimisation has not been performed comprehensively for the specific 
3 
applications, thus affecting the accuracy of predicted combustion properties in practical applications. 
4 
Therefore, our framework incorporates three novel and synergistic advances that distinguish it from 
5 
conventional methods and substantially enhances the prediction of chemical kinetic mechanisms for 
6 
practical applications: (i) the use of MOO, specifically Multi-Objective Particle Swarm Optimisation 
7 
(MOPSO), to simultaneously balance accuracy and consistency across datasets at diverse 
8 
thermochemical conditions; (ii) a novel treatment of uncertainty by retaining all experimental 
9 
datapoints and incorporating their deviation directly into the optimisation objectives; and (iii) the use 
10 
of full chemical kinetic simulations for all candidate solutions, made feasible by deploying the 
11 
framework on an HPC platform. This is the first effort to combine all three elements, establishing a 
12 
novel approach for robust, data-rich mechanism optimisation that moves beyond the conventional use 
13 
of single-objective formulations, fixed-bound filtering, or response surface-based approximations. 
14 
Therefore, this work presents a new chemical kinetic mechanism optimisation framework with two 
15 
objective functions – to maximise the number of datapoints modelled within their uncertainty bounds 
16 
and to minimise the normalised Root Mean Square Error (nRMSE) between predicted and 
17 
experimental values. The framework utilises a MOPSO to explore the uncertainty hyperspace with the 
18 
full chemical kinetic simulations handled by an HPC facility. To demonstrate the potential of the new 
19 
approach, the framework is applied to a newly assembled H2-NOx mechanism using an extensive 
20 
experimental dataset of combustion targets covering a broad range of thermochemical conditions – a 
21 
total of 118 fundamental combustion datasets containing 1695 datapoints were used. The lower 
22 
computational load of the MOPSO enables to perform the optimisation without surrogate models, 
23 
thus eliminating any errors introduced by the solution mapping approach. To further validate the 
24 
optimised mechanism, it was applied to model secondary experimental engine data from a 
25 


 
 
6 
 
Cooperative Fuel Research (CFR) F1/F2 engine operating under lean conditions in Homogeneous 
1 
Charge Compression Ignition (HCCI) mode.

5

7

2. Framework Definition 
12 
This section describes the optimisation framework, which is based on a MOPSO with two objective 
13 
functions aiming to maximise the number of target datapoints simulated within their uncertainty limits 
14 
and to minimise the modelling errors across the entire dataset collected. The MOPSO algorithm was 
15 
selected over previously used approaches, such as Genetic Algorithms, because it offers substantially 
16 
lower computational cost while maintaining effective exploration of the Pareto front. For example, the 
17 
GA implementation in [38] required 1,000 generations with 60 individuals per generation, amounting 
18 
to 60,000 model evaluations. In contrast, an MOPSO run with 256 particles converged within an 
19 
average of 24 iterations, requiring only 6,144 model evaluations. This represents nearly a tenfold 
20 
reduction in computational effort compared to the GA. The optimisation framework was implemented 
21 
on the GW4 Isambard HPC [55] with the full kinetic simulations handled by Cantera v3.0.0 [56].

Validation Data and Numerical Modelling 
7 
The mechanism was optimised using a dataset based on the dataset from [60] with additional 
8

4. Framework Application 
1 
As the MOPSO algorithm cannot guarantee the discovery of globally optimal solutions for the objective 
2 
functions, the optimisation of the chemical kinetic mechanism employed a multistage approach. This 
3 
approach aimed to identify multiple local optima initially and then refine the search range to focus on 
4 
a smaller number of the best candidates. The optimisation was performed in three simulation stages 
5 
followed by a final analysis stage. Each MOPSO instance used 256 particles and was executed on the 
6 
Isambard HPC facility [55] facility, which comprises 336 Marvell ThunderX2 32-core CPUs (21,504 
7 
Armv8 cores in total). MOPSO runs were parallelised across 2048 cores (32 CPUs) resulting in an 
8 
average runtime of circa 30 minutes per iteration and approximately 12 hours per MOPSO instance. 
9 
As detailed below, a total of 45 MOPSO instances were computed. 
10 
Stage 1. The first simulation stage consisted of 25 MOPSO runs and explored the uncertainty 
11 
hyperspace with the goal of finding a large amount of local nRMSE minima and UF maxima. During this 
12 
stage, the particles in the MOPSO runs were instantiated at random locations, thus promoting the 
13 
exploration of the uncertainty hyperspace. The combined repositories produced 139 unique locations 
14 
in the hyperspace.  
15 
Stage 2. The second simulation stage consisted of 10 MOPSO runs and aimed to hone into the best 
16 
local nRMSE minima and UF maxima identified in the first stage. During this stage, the particles were 
17 
instantiated at the 139 unique locations identified in the first stage. As 256 particles were used in each 
18 
instance of the MOPSO, the 139 locations were duplicated and then truncated to 256. Following this 
19 
stage, the unique locations of interest were reduced to 96 nondominated locations.  
20 
Stage 3. The third simulation stage consisted of 10 MOPSO runs and aimed to explore the uncertainty 
21 
hyperspace in proximity to the nondominated locations identified in the previous stage. The 256 
22 
particles were instantiated in the locations of the repository particles of the second stage, following 
23 
their duplication and truncation. The repositories of these 10 runs contained 330 particle locations in 
24 


 
 
23 
 
total. Note that while the final stage produced the most nondominated particles, they were staggered 
1 
around a handful of local optima.

8. Conclusion 
9 
This comprehensive study has introduced a new framework for chemical kinetic mechanism 
10 
optimisation using a multi-objective particle swarm optimisation algorithm. In contrast to the existing 
11 
approaches, this framework considered the number of predictions falling within the measurement 
12 
uncertainty limits as a second objective, resulting in a much higher fidelity of the optimised 
13 
mechanism. Additionally, all representative experimental results were included in the optimisation, 
14 
covering a wide range of thermodynamic conditions, especially those of interest to practical hydrogen 
15 
combustion applications. Finally, direct kinetic modelling of combustion properties was implemented 
16 
on the HPC facility, which greatly reduced the errors in evaluating the objective functions, especially 
17 
comparing with the commonly used response surface approach. 
18 
As a demonstration of the efficacy and new insights that can be gained from the new framework, it 
19 
was applied to the optimisation of a H2-NOx chemical kinetic mechanism, in which the uncertainty 
20 
hyperspace of the pre-exponential coefficients of 34 reactions was explored. The detailed optimised 
21 
mechanism, termed Bath-H2, reproduced the optimisation data with higher accuracy than existing 
22

1 
temperatures and intermediate pressures was driven by several factors. In an RCM, the overall lower 
2 
net production rate of ȮH radicals in the early stages of the combustion system resulted in an increased 
3 
ignition delay time compared to the baseline. In an NO2-doped system in a shock tube, the improved 
4 
fit was attributed to changes in the NO-NO2 interconversion cycle with the 30% increase in the pre-
5 
exponential coefficient of NO2+ḢóNO+ȮH leading to higher ȮH concentrations in the early stages of 
6 
the combustion system and hence earlier autoignition.

8 
mechanism predicted autoignition within an internal combustion engine with similar accuracy to 
9 
current state-of-the-art mechanisms for data without NO in the intake mixture and with significantly 
10 
increased accuracy for data with NO in the intake mixture. This highlights the need to incorporate 
11 
engine data featuring transient conditions in chemical kinetic mechanism optimisation strategies in 
12 
order to enable the development of mechanisms with higher accuracy to practical combustion 
13 
systems. In summary, this new framework opens a new area of research combining accurate modelling 
14 
of combustion processes to understand the underlying chemical kinetic mechanisms, thus enabling 
15
